claim: In flies, the direction of moving ON and OFF features is computed separately.
source: In flies, the direction of moving ON and OFF features is computed separately.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction regarding separate ON and OFF pathways.

claim: T4 (ON) and T5 (OFF) are the first neurons in their respective pathways to extract a directionally selective response from their non-selective inputs.
source: T4 (ON) and T5 (OFF) are the first neurons in their respective pathways to extract a directionally selective response from their non-selective inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Maisak et al., 2013; Serbe et al., 2016; Strother et al., 2017).

claim: T4 neurons integrate offset depolarizing and hyperpolarizing inputs to generate directional selectivity.
source: Our recent study of T4 found that the integration of offset depolarizing and hyperpolarizing inputs is critical for the generation of directional selectivity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and refers to the authors' previous study (Gruntman et al., 2018).

claim: T5 neurons lack small-field inhibitory inputs.
source: However, T5s lack small-field inhibitory inputs, suggesting they may use a different mechanism.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by connectomics and transcriptomic data cited in the introduction (Shinomiya et al., 2019; Davis et al., 2018).

claim: T5 neurons have a receptive field structure with fast depolarization and persistent, spatially offset hyperpolarization.
source: Here we used whole-cell recordings of T5 neurons and found a similar receptive field structure: fast depolarization and persistent, spatially offset hyperpolarization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: T5 neurons show only suppressive responses to non-preferred motion direction, with no amplifying responses.
source: By assaying pairwise interactions of local stimulation across the receptive field, we found no amplifying responses, only suppressive responses to the non-preferred motion direction.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: A passive biophysical model using direct inhibition can accurately predict T5 responses to moving stimuli.
source: We then evaluated passive, biophysical models and found that a model using direct inhibition, but not the removal of excitation, can accurately predict T5 responses to a range of moving stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by modeling results in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: A model based on removal of excitation cannot accurately predict T5 responses to moving stimuli.
source: We then evaluated passive, biophysical models and found that a model using direct inhibition, but not the removal of excitation, can accurately predict T5 responses to a range of moving stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by modeling results in Figure 6.

claim: All models for generating directionally selective responses share three common elements: spatially offset inputs, temporal asymmetry between them, and non-linear combination.
source: Although several different models have been proposed for generating directionally selective responses across species, they all share three common elements: (1) spatially offset inputs with a (2) temporal asymmetry between them, that are (3) non-linearly combined.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a general principle of motion detection models.

claim: Directional selectivity can be generated by enhancing responses in the preferred direction.
source: These models generate Directional Selectivity (DS) by enhancing responses in the preferred direction (seen in flies: Fisher et al., 2015; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016), suppressing responses in the null, or non-preferred direction, or by a combination of both (also from flies; Haag et al., 2016; Leong et al., 2016; Strother et al., 2017, reviewed in Yang and Clandinin, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Directional selectivity can be generated by suppressing responses in the null direction.
source: These models generate Directional Selectivity (DS) by enhancing responses in the preferred direction (seen in flies: Fisher et al., 2015; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016), suppressing responses in the null, or non-preferred direction, or by a combination of both (also from flies; Haag et al., 2016; Leong et al., 2016; Strother et al., 2017, reviewed in Yang and Clandinin, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Local luminance increments (ON) and decrements (OFF) are processed by largely separate circuits in flies.
source: In flies, local luminance increments (ON) and decrements (OFF) are processed by largely separate circuits, with motion being computed separately in each pathway (Behnia et al., 2014; Clark et al., 2011; Franceschini et al., 1989; Joesch et al., 2010; Silies et al., 2013; Strother et al., 2014; Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: T4 neurons use both local excitatory and inhibitory inputs to generate directionally selective responses.
source: T4 neurons use both local excitatory and inhibitory inputs to generate directionally selective responses (Gruntman et al., 2018; Haag et al., 2017; Strother et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: All columnar inputs to T5 neurons depolarize in response to OFF stimuli.
source: A recent connectomics study has characterized all the columnar inputs to T5 neurons (Shinomiya et al., 2019) and a functional imaging study revealed they all depolarize in response to OFF stimuli (Serbe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: All columnar inputs to T5 neurons are cholinergic.
source: However, transcriptional profiling of these neuron types shows that these inputs are all cholinergic, and therefore unlikely to provide local inhibitory input (Davis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citation.

claim: Cholinergic inputs are unlikely to provide local inhibitory input to T5 neurons.
source: However, transcriptional profiling of these neuron types shows that these inputs are all cholinergic, and therefore unlikely to provide local inhibitory input (Davis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from transcriptional profiling data.

claim: T5 neurons show clear preferred and null directions of motion with relatively wide tuning.
source: Each of the 17 T5 neurons we recorded showed clear preferred and null directions (PD and ND) of motion, with relatively wide tuning (i.e. similar magnitude responses in the directions ± 45° away from the PD; individual neuron example Figure 1D; population responses Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: T5 preferred direction responses show clear hyperpolarization following the depolarizing peak.
source: The PD response shows a clear hyperpolarization following the depolarizing peak, and the ND response shows a dip preceding the depolarization peak.
evidence: This is stated in the results and can be observed in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: T5 null direction responses show a dip preceding the depolarization peak.
source: The PD response shows a clear hyperpolarization following the depolarizing peak, and the ND response shows a dip preceding the depolarization peak.
evidence: This is stated in the results and can be observed in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: The smallest bar presented (1-pixel wide, ~2°) generated a clear directionally selective response in T5 neurons.
source: We note that the smallest bar presented (1-pixel wide,~2°) generated a clear directionally selective response but did not induce the prominent hyperpolarization observed for the wider bars.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The smallest bar presented did not induce prominent hyperpolarization in T5 neurons.
source: We note that the smallest bar presented (1-pixel wide,~2°) generated a clear directionally selective response but did not induce the prominent hyperpolarization observed for the wider bars.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Wider bars evoked stronger responses in T5 neurons but did not increase the DSI.
source: We further note that although wider bars evoked stronger responses, they did not increase the DSI (Figure 1E), because these stronger stimuli also evoked a corresponding increase in the ND response magnitude.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: T5 receptive field is comprised of depolarizing responses dominating the center with increased response magnitude for stronger stimuli.
source: Aligning the responses from all the cells based on the position of the peak depolarization (Figure 2A) reveals T5's (first-order) RF structure: (1) Depolarizing responses dominate the center, with increased response magnitude for stronger stimuli (wider bars or flashes of longer duration).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: T5 inputs along the PD-ND axis are spatially asymmetric around the RF center.
source: (2) Inputs along the PD-ND axis are spatially asymmetric around the RF center. On the leading side of the RF the responses reflect depolarizing input (Figure 2A, green positions), while on the trailing side, responses show a mixture of depolarization and hyperpolarization (Figure 2A, pink positions).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: On the leading side of the T5 RF, responses reflect depolarizing input.
source: On the leading side of the RF the responses reflect depolarizing input (Figure 2A, green positions), while on the trailing side, responses show a mixture of depolarization and hyperpolarization (Figure 2A, pink positions).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: On the trailing side of the T5 RF, responses show a mixture of depolarization and hyperpolarization.
source: On the leading side of the RF the responses reflect depolarizing input (Figure 2A, green positions), while on the trailing side, responses show a mixture of depolarization and hyperpolarization (Figure 2A, pink positions).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The T5 receptive field structure is similar to T5 measurements using voltage imaging.
source: This general structure is similar to T5 measurements in a recent paper using voltage imaging (Wienecke et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation.

claim: Long duration responses on the leading side of T5 RF show a plateau-like depolarization peak.
source: Long duration responses on the leading side show a plateau-like depolarization peak, while responses on the trailing side show a peak that rapidly decays (Figure 2B, pink vs. green responses).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Responses on the trailing side of T5 RF show a peak that rapidly decays.
source: Long duration responses on the leading side show a plateau-like depolarization peak, while responses on the trailing side show a peak that rapidly decays (Figure 2B, pink vs. green responses).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Rapidly decaying response peaks in T5 likely arise from competition between fast-rising, fast-decaying depolarizing inputs and slow-rising, slow-decaying hyperpolarizing inputs.
source: These decaying response peaks likely arise from a 'competition' between fast-rising, fast-decaying depolarizing inputs and slow-rising, slow-decaying hyperpolarizing inputs.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Spatially asymmetric hyperpolarization induces faster decaying responses on the T5 RF's trailing side.
source: Spatially asymmetric hyperpolarization also induces faster decaying responses on the RF's trailing side (Figure 2B pink vs. green, quantified in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: In T4 neurons, asymmetric, slow-decaying hyperpolarization is the main contributor to DS generation.
source: In T4 neurons, we showed that the asymmetric, slow-decaying hyperpolarization is the main contributor to DS generation, since ND movement first activates the faster-decaying depolarizing response components, which in turn lead to less efficient summation and smaller net depolarization (Gruntman et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the results and supported by citation to the authors' previous work.

claim: Faster decay times on the trailing side of T5 neurons are likely the result of hyperpolarization temporally sharpening responses.
source: Therefore, the faster decay times on the trailing side of T5 neurons were also the likely result of hyperpolarization temporally sharpening responses.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an inference based on comparison with T4 neurons.

claim: Trailing-side responses in T5 started sooner and rose faster than leading-side responses.
source: Unlike in T4, trailing-side responses started sooner and rose faster than leading-side responses (Figure 2C; two-tailed t-tests, p<0.05 for all conditions).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2C with statistical testing.

claim: The T5 RF structure is comparable to the RF structure measured for T4 cells.
source: This structure is comparable to the RF structure we measured for T4 cells (Figure 2D, black curves).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: T5 responses on the leading side of the RF, up to and including the center, did not exhibit directional selectivity.
source: Responses on the leading side of the RF, up to and including the center (position 0), did not exhibit DS. Since both PD and ND combinations evoke a similar maximal response (e.g. −3 to −1 versus −1 to −3, horizontal lines) the neurons are effectively 'motion blind' in this region of the RF.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: T5 neurons are effectively 'motion blind' in the leading side region of the RF.
source: Since both PD and ND combinations evoke a similar maximal response (e.g. −3 to −1 versus −1 to −3, horizontal lines) the neurons are effectively 'motion blind' in this region of the RF.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Responses to combinations that included the trailing side of the T5 RF exhibited a larger maximal response for the PD combination.
source: Responses to combinations that included the trailing side of the RF, where hyperpolarization was detected (Figure 2D), exhibited a larger maximal response for the PD combination, and therefore exhibited DS (e.g. Figure 3B 1 to 3 in red versus 3 to 1 in blue, horizontal lines).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No combinations of 4.5° bars showed PD enhancement in T5 neurons.
source: We note that there are no conditions where the summed responses are smaller than the measured responses, regardless of whether the comparison is made using response maximum or mean (Figure 3—figure supplement 1). In other words, no combinations of 4.5° bars showed PD enhancement.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: T5 findings of no PD enhancement hold for all apparent motion conditions tested: fast (40 ms) and slow (160 ms), bars of width 2 (4.5°) and width 4 (9°), and sequential positions that were either adjacent or overlapping.
source: However, our findings hold for all of the apparent motion conditions we tested: fast (40 ms) and slow (160 ms), bars of width 2 (4.5°) and width 4 (9°), and sequential positions that were either adjacent or overlapping (Figure 3D,E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D, 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a significant correlation between the magnitude of ND suppression and the magnitude of the directionally selective response in T5 neurons.
source: Furthermore, we found a significant correlation between the magnitude of ND suppression and the magnitude of the directionally selective response (more suppression correlates with more DS), while no such correlation was found for PD responses (Figure 3E; MeasuredND - SumND vs. MaxPD - MaxND R2: 0.396, slope 95% confidence interval: [−0.64,–0.31]; MeasuredPD - SumPD vs. MaxPD - MaxND R2: 0.02, slope 95% confidence interval: [−0.402, 0.073]).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: There is no correlation between PD responses and the magnitude of the directionally selective response in T5 neurons.
source: Furthermore, we found a significant correlation between the magnitude of ND suppression and the magnitude of the directionally selective response (more suppression correlates with more DS), while no such correlation was found for PD responses (Figure 3E; MeasuredND - SumND vs. MaxPD - MaxND R2: 0.396, slope 95% confidence interval: [−0.64,–0.31]; MeasuredPD - SumPD vs. MaxPD - MaxND R2: 0.02, slope 95% confidence interval: [−0.402, 0.073]).
evidence: This is stated in the results with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The data provide strong evidence for the suppression of ND motion as the only mechanism through which DS is generated in the membrane potential of T5 neurons.
source: Taken together, these data provide strong evidence for the suppression of ND motion as the only mechanism through which DS is generated in the membrane potential of T5 neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the data in Figure 3.

claim: The EI model includes an excitatory and an inhibitory conductance that are combined using a biophysically inspired non-linearity.
source: The model—henceforth referred to as the EI model—includes an excitatory and an inhibitory conductance that are combined using a biophysically inspired non-linearity (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the model.

claim: The EI model is parameterized with spatial and temporal filters for each conductance.
source: The model—henceforth referred to as the EI model—includes an excitatory and an inhibitory conductance that are combined using a biophysically inspired non-linearity (Figure 4A). The model, which is slightly simplified from our previous T4 model (Gruntman et al., 2018), is parameterized with spatial and temporal filters for each conductance (Supplementary file 1 and Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the model.

claim: Passive integration of excitatory and inhibitory conductances is sufficient to explain T5's response dynamics.
source: Based on our previous T4 modeling (Gruntman et al., 2018), we hypothesized that the passive integration of these conductances would be sufficient to explain T5's response dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a hypothesis tested by the model.

claim: The EI model predicts the magnitude and dynamics of T5 responses to all three bar widths.
source: Figure 4B shows the results from an example cell, with the recorded responses and model prediction overlaid for three bar widths and with both fast and slow flash durations. The model predicts the magnitude and dynamics of the responses to all three widths, with no systematic difference for the larger or smaller width bars.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The linear model predictions consistently overestimate T5 response magnitudes.
source: The linear model predictions capture some of the response dynamics but appear to overestimate response magnitudes, particularly for strong stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D and 4E.

claim: The EI model captures both the magnitude of the maximal response in both directions and the dynamic structure of the response traces to moving bars.
source: Our EI model, on the other hand, captures both the magnitude of the maximal response in both directions and the dynamic structure of the response traces.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The EI model accurately predicted responses to grating flashes.
source: As can be seen from the example cell (same cell and parameters as in Figure 4), our model also accurately predicted responses to these grating flashes.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The EI model's predictions capture the transient responses to the appearance of drifting gratings.
source: Although the model parameters were optimized using only the static stimuli responses (Figure 4B, middle), the model's predictions capture several aspects of the recorded responses: the transient responses to the appearance of the grating (that differ dramatically between the two phases), the amplitude of the oscillation (compared in Figure 5E), and even the apparent amplitude adaptation in the responses to fast-drifting gratings.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The EI model's predictions capture the amplitude of the oscillation in responses to drifting gratings.
source: Although the model parameters were optimized using only the static stimuli responses (Figure 4B, middle), the model's predictions capture several aspects of the recorded responses: the transient responses to the appearance of the grating (that differ dramatically between the two phases), the amplitude of the oscillation (compared in Figure 5E), and even the apparent amplitude adaptation in the responses to fast-drifting gratings.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The EI model's predictions capture the apparent amplitude adaptation in the responses to fast-drifting gratings.
source: Although the model parameters were optimized using only the static stimuli responses (Figure 4B, middle), the model's predictions capture several aspects of the recorded responses: the transient responses to the appearance of the grating (that differ dramatically between the two phases), the amplitude of the oscillation (compared in Figure 5E), and even the apparent amplitude adaptation in the responses to fast-drifting gratings.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The E+E- model fails to generalize to wider bar flash stimuli.
source: Although the E+E- model predicts the response magnitude for the bar width two stimuli that were used in the optimization, it fails to generalize, as evidenced by poor estimates of responses to wider bar flash stimuli (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A and 6B.

claim: The E+E- model predictions for moving bar stimuli consistently overestimate the measured responses.
source: The E+E- model predictions for moving bar stimuli also consistently overestimate the measured responses, with larger errors in the responses to ND stimuli (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The directional selectivity of the E+E- model is lower than measured in T5 neurons.
source: The differential overestimation of ND responses means that response magnitudes to bars moving in the preferred or the null direction are similar. As a consequence, the directional selectivity of the E+E- model is lower than measured (DSI for the example cell indicated in Figure 6C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Removing excitation is qualitatively different from adding inhibition in generating directional selectivity.
source: This model comparison shows that removing excitation is qualitatively different from adding inhibition.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the model comparison in Figure 7.

claim: The EI model amplifies the differences between the PD and ND responses by normalizing the difference between the depolarizing and hyperpolarizing conductances with their sum.
source: By normalizing the difference between the depolarizing and hyperpolarizing conductances with their sum, the EI model amplifies the differences between the PD and ND responses (already present in the ΔG).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an explanation of the model's mechanism.

claim: Inhibition appears to sculpt the essential asymmetry for directionally selective responses in T5 cells.
source: Taken together, these modeling results corroborate our central finding that inhibition appears to sculpt the essential asymmetry for directionally selective responses in T5 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the modeling analysis.

claim: T4 and T5 share a high degree of anatomical similarity.
source: T4 and T5 share a high degree of anatomical similarity (Fischbach and Dittrich, 1989; Shinomiya et al., 2019; Strausfeld and Lee, 1991; Takemura et al., 2017; Takemura et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Both T4 and T5 receive four major columnar inputs.
source: Focusing only on their dendrites, both neuron types receive four major columnar inputs, both preferentially synapse onto neurons of their same subtype, and both receive prominent input from CT1, a single, large GABAergic interneuron (Shinomiya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: Both T4 and T5 preferentially synapse onto neurons of their same subtype.
source: Focusing only on their dendrites, both neuron types receive four major columnar inputs, both preferentially synapse onto neurons of their same subtype, and both receive prominent input from CT1, a single, large GABAergic interneuron (Shinomiya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: Both T4 and T5 receive prominent input from CT1, a single, large GABAergic interneuron.
source: Focusing only on their dendrites, both neuron types receive four major columnar inputs, both preferentially synapse onto neurons of their same subtype, and both receive prominent input from CT1, a single, large GABAergic interneuron (Shinomiya et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: T4 receives mixed inputs from columnar cholinergic, GABAergic, and Glutamatergic cells.
source: However, the described anatomy of the T4 and T5 inputs, combined with transcriptomic data (Davis et al., 2018), shows that T4 receives mixed inputs from columnar cholinergic, GABAergic, and Glutamatergic cells, while all columnar inputs to T5 are cholinergic.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: The DS generation mechanism in T4 and T5 appears to be all but identical: fast depolarization with asymmetric slow hyperpolarization on the trailing side of the RF.
source: This substantial difference between the inputs of these two cells is especially surprising since the DS generation mechanism in T4 and T5 appears to be all but identical: fast depolarization with asymmetric slow hyperpolarization on the trailing side of the RF.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental results.

claim: CT1 may function like a small-field, columnar neuron and provide the necessary local inhibitory input to T5.
source: A potential source for this input is CT1 that was thought to provide only non-local inhibitory inputs due to its morphology. However, a recent study raises the possibility that CT1 may function like a small-field, columnar neuron and provide the necessary local inhibitory input (Meier and Borst, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: T5 neurons express several GABA receptors.
source: In agreement with this proposal, transcriptomic profiling shows that T5 neurons express several GABA receptors (Davis et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: Some fraction of the cholinergic inputs to T5 could activate an inhibitory conductance.
source: A further possibility is that some fraction of the cholinergic inputs could activate an inhibitory conductance (first proposed in Shinomiya et al., 2014 ), in which case the T4 model should apply to T5, but be understood to make use of a rather different molecular implementation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a possibility and supported by citation.

claim: No evidence was found for a PD-enhancing mechanism in T5 neurons, even with stronger stimuli.
source: First, we found no evidence for a PD-enhancing mechanism in T5 neurons, even with stronger stimuli as was previously shown with calcium imaging (Haag et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: When both calcium and voltage responses were imaged in T5 neurons, amplification was found only in the calcium signal.
source: When both calcium and voltage responses were imaged in T5 neurons, Wienecke et al. (2018) found amplification only in the calcium signal, and this amplification was proposed to emerge from the transformation of membrane voltage to fluorescent calcium signals.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: The model proposed by Wienecke et al. (2018) is based on a voltage signal that is integrated linearly across the cell's receptive field.
source: However, the model proposed by Wienecke et al. (2018) is based on a voltage signal that is integrated linearly across the cell's receptive field; this linear signal is then amplified or suppressed by a 1 degree of freedom, non-linear, voltage-to-calcium transformation (Figure 8, left column).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by citation.

claim: Electrophysiological measurements show that T5 voltage signals do not simply integrate linearly but are reliably sublinear.
source: Our electrophysiological measurements show that the voltage signals do not simply integrate linearly but are reliably sublinear (see for example Figures 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by data in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The EI model implements a 2 degree of freedom nonlinearity that results in ND suppression in the voltage signal.
source: The right column shows a unifying proposal in which our EI model implements a 2 dof nonlinearity (dofs represented by ΔG and ΣG, see Figure 7) that results in ND suppression in the voltage signal.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 8.

claim: The EI model does not explain the PD enhancement observed in calcium measurements.
source: Since our model does not explain the PD enhancement observed in calcium measurements (e.g. Fisher et al., 2015; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2016; Haag et al., 2016), we augment this model with a voltage-to-calcium transformation.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 8.

claim: A secondary mechanism relating the transformation of membrane voltage to calcium in the axon terminals could further enhance signals for PD motion and suppress signals for ND motion.
source: Subsequent to this, a secondary mechanism that relates the transformation of membrane voltage to calcium in the axon terminals could further enhance signals for PD motion and suppress signals for ND motion using an additional nonlinearity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposed unifying framework.

claim: Experiments were performed on 1–2 day old female Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Experiments were performed on 1–2 day old female Drosophila melanogaster (flies were reared under 16:8 light:dark cycle at 24°C).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: All recordings were obtained from the left side of the brain.
source: All recordings were obtained from the left side of the brain.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The display covered slightly more than one half of a cylinder (216° in azimuth and ~72° in elevation) of the fly's visual field.
source: The arena covered slightly more than one half of a cylinder (216° in azimuth and ~72° in elevation) of the fly's visual field, with the diameter of each pixel subtending an angle of (at most) 2.25° on the fly eye.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Green LEDs with emission peak at 565 nm were used for visual stimulation.
source: Green LEDs (emission peak: 565 nm) were used, dark stimuli (off pixels) were presented on an intermediate intensity background of ~31 cd/m2.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Dark stimuli were presented on an intermediate intensity background of ~31 cd/m2.
source: Green LEDs (emission peak: 565 nm) were used, dark stimuli (off pixels) were presented on an intermediate intensity background of ~31 cd/m2.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.
